summary.text: For consecutive divisors \(x<y\), the condition that \(y\) is odd and \(y\ge 2x\) is equivalent to \(y>2x\): oddness rules out equality, while if \(y>2x\) were even then \(y/2\) would be a divisor strictly between \(x\) and \(y\), contradicting consecutiveness. Thus the counted terms are exactly the breaks between maximal 2-dense blocks, whose number is one plus the number of such breaks.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\ge 1\), and write its positive divisors in strictly increasing order as
\[
  1=d_1<d_2<\cdots<d_m=n.
\]
Thus \(m\ge 1\). We use the following divisor characterization of A237271: if \(a(n)\) denotes the number of parts in the symmetric representation of \(\sigma(n)\), then
\[
 a(n)=1+\#\bigl\{i:1\le i<m,\ d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr\}.
 \tag{1}
\]
In other words, apart from the initial part, a new part in the symmetric representation is counted at a consecutive pair of divisors \((d_i,d_{i+1})\) precisely when the latter divisor is odd and is at least twice the former. We will prove that the set counted in (1) is exactly the set of breaks between maximal \(2\)-dense sublists.

The key point is the following equivalence, valid for every consecutive pair \(d_i,d_{i+1}\):
\[
 \bigl(d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 d_{i+1}>2d_i.
 \tag{2}
\]

First suppose that \(d_{i+1}\) is odd and \(d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\). Equality cannot occur, because \(2d_i\) is even whereas \(d_{i+1}\) is odd. Hence the inequality is strict, and \(d_{i+1}>2d_i\).

Conversely, suppose that
\[
 d_{i+1}>2d_i.
 \tag{3}
\]
This certainly gives \(d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\), so it remains only to prove that \(d_{i+1}\) is odd. Assume for contradiction that \(d_{i+1}\) is even. Write
\[
 d_{i+1}=2k
\]
for a positive integer \(k\). Since \(d_{i+1}\mid n\) and \(k\mid d_{i+1}\), transitivity of divisibility gives \(k\mid n\). Thus \(k\) is itself one of the divisors in the displayed ordered list. Moreover, (3) becomes
\[
 2k>2d_i,
\]
so \(k>d_i\). Also \(k<2k=d_{i+1}\), because \(k>0\). Consequently
\[
 d_i<k<d_{i+1},
\]
with \(k\mid n\). This is impossible because \(d_i\) and \(d_{i+1}\) are consecutive in the increasing list of all divisors of \(n\): no divisor of \(n\) can lie strictly between them. Therefore \(d_{i+1}\) cannot be even, and hence it is odd. This proves the reverse implication and establishes (2).

We now relate the strict inequalities in (2) to maximal \(2\)-dense sublists. Call an index \(i\), with \(1\le i<m\), a break if
\[
 d_{i+1}>2d_i.
 \tag{4}
\]
At every index which is not a break we have
\[
 d_{i+1}\le 2d_i,
\]
which is exactly the condition that this adjacent pair may remain inside a \(2\)-dense sublist. At a break, on the other hand, \(d_i\) and \(d_{i+1}\) cannot belong to the same contiguous \(2\)-dense sublist.

For completeness, the maximal sublists can be constructed explicitly from these breaks. Cut the ordered divisor list immediately after every \(d_i\) for which (4) holds. The resulting pieces are nonempty contiguous sublists. Inside any one piece there was no cut, so every consecutive pair \((d_j,d_{j+1})\) in that piece satisfies \(d_{j+1}\le 2d_j\); therefore every piece is \(2\)-dense. Each such piece is maximal. Indeed, if it is not the first piece, the adjacent divisor immediately preceding it is separated from its first term by a break, so adjoining that divisor would violate the factor-at-most-\(2\) condition. Likewise, if it is not the last piece, the pair consisting of its final term and the next divisor is a break, so the piece cannot be extended to the right.

Conversely, every maximal contiguous \(2\)-dense sublist must be one of these pieces. It cannot cross a break, because the adjacent pair at that break violates the defining inequality. It also cannot stop at a non-break unless it is already at the end of the full divisor list, because at a non-break the next divisor could be adjoined while preserving \(2\)-density, contradicting maximality. The same reasoning applies to its left endpoint. Thus cutting at the breaks gives exactly, and not merely some of, the maximal \(2\)-dense sublists.

Because the original divisor list is nonempty, before any cuts it consists of one piece. Each break introduces exactly one additional piece. Hence
\[
 \#\{\text{maximal \(2\)-dense sublists of the divisors of }n\}
 =1+\#\bigl\{i:1\le i<m,\ d_{i+1}>2d_i\bigr\}.
 \tag{5}
\]
By the equivalence (2), the set on the right-hand side of (5) is exactly
\[
 \bigl\{i:1\le i<m,\ d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr\}.
\]
Substituting this into (5) and comparing with the divisor characterization (1) yields
\[
 \#\{\text{maximal \(2\)-dense sublists of divisors of }n\}=a(n).
\]

The endpoint case \(n=1\) is included: the divisor list is the one-term list \([1]\), there are no adjacent pairs and hence no breaks, so both (1) and (5) give the value \(1\). Therefore, for every \(n\ge1\), the number of parts in the symmetric representation of \(\sigma(n)\) is exactly the number of maximal sublists of consecutive divisors of \(n\) whose successive terms increase by a factor of at most \(2\).
